meta.title: Cosmos Health: educational simulation data
meta.purpose: A spaceflight health education simulation using synthetic values and cited NASA/CSA context. The simulated pattern display is project-authored and does not determine real causes or individual risk.
meta.noThresholds: The listed NASA/CSA sources do not provide universal clinical thresholds for these indicators. Demo defaults and slider bounds are project-authored interface settings only.

resourceCoverage.note: The official Resources tab listed three NASA resources and two CSA partner resources. JAXA is retained as supplementary source material only; it was not among the five listed links.

meta.prototypeNotice: Simulation mode: all displayed values are synthetic. The hazard pattern is a simplified, project-authored demonstration—not a NASA score, probability, diagnosis, causal finding, or medical recommendation. Do not enter real health information.
meta.emergencyCopy: For urgent symptoms or immediate danger, follow the appropriate emergency procedures and contact qualified medical support. Do not rely on this simulation.
meta.assetAttributionReview: Source and license details for local images and font/CDN assets are not established in this dataset; confirm and list them in challenge submission references.
meta.bodyHazardMappingMethod: Body-topic hazard links are derived only from hazardLinks in cited NASA risk records listed in that body panel’s riskRefs. If the source record has no explicit hazardLinks, no body-to-hazard link is shown. These links are educational context, not individual causation.

pageNotes.note: The five hazards can feed off one another and worsen effects on the human body.
The effects of the risks vary depending on whether humans travel to low Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars.
The risks page groups the 17 risks into three sets: human physiology (11), behavioral performance and human factors (5), and space radiation (1).
Neither NASA page gives normal ranges, thresholds or measurement procedures for any health indicator.

hazards.name: Space radiation
hazards.summary: Invisible to the human eye and considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

hazards.name: Isolation and confinement
hazards.summary: Behavioral responses occur among groups of people far from Earth who are isolated and confined in a small space over a long period.
additionalFacts: Crews must be carefully chosen, trained and supported to work effectively as a team for months or years in space.

hazards.name: Distance from Earth
hazards.summary: Instructions, new supplies, medical care and more become harder to receive from Earth as astronauts venture deeper into space.
additionalFacts: Mars is on average 140 million miles from Earth; astronauts would leave for roughly three years instead of a three-day lunar trip.
Planning and self-sufficiency are key to successful deep-space missions.

hazards.name: Gravity fields
hazards.summary: Muscles, bones, inner ear and organs must adjust to the new gravities met on the station or spacecraft, on the Moon, on Mars, and on Earth after returning home.
additionalFacts: On Mars astronauts would live and work in three-eighths of Earth's gravitational pull for up to two years.

hazards.name: Hostile and closed environments
hazards.summary: Keeping a spacecraft ecosystem safe means managing temperature, pressure and lighting, reducing noise, monitoring microbial communities and tracking immune responses.
additionalFacts: Habitability factors NASA names: temperature, pressure, lighting, noise and the presence of microbes.

risks.name: Altered immune system responses
risks.summary: Spaceflight stresses can reactivate dormant viruses in astronauts, causing rashes and other symptoms; work continues on understanding immune changes.

hazardLinks.basis: hazards page: lists tracking immune responses under hostile/closed environments

risks.name: Altered sensorimotor and vestibular function
risks.summary: Astronauts can have motion sickness, trouble with hand-eye or gait coordination, and dizziness during gravity changes, which can make walking or operating a vehicle hard.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page: occurs during gravitational changes

risks.name: Cardiovascular adaptations
risks.summary: Weightlessness alters blood circulation and heart and blood-vessel function, potentially raising the risk of cardiovascular events.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page: attributes the change to weightlessness

risks.name: Decompression sickness
risks.summary: Moving from a pressurized spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit can make dissolved nitrogen bubble in body tissues, causing health and mission problems.

risks.name: Host-microorganism interactions
risks.summary: Skin and gut microbiomes can change in space, potentially raising crews' risk of getting sick.

hazardLinks.basis: hazards page: lists monitoring microbial communities under hostile/closed environments

risks.name: Hypoxia
risks.summary: Steps to avoid decompression sickness on future deep-space spacewalks also raise the risk of mild hypoxia, meaning lower-than-normal oxygen in body tissues.

risks.name: Inadequate food and nutrition
risks.summary: A healthy, balanced diet is essential to crew health and performance; research targets enjoyable, long-lasting, nutritious meals and the consequences of inadequate nutrition.

risks.name: Injury and compromised performance from spacewalks
risks.summary: Suit work is challenging: besides cognitive fatigue and injury, crews manage spacewalk-environment risks including decompression sickness and low oxygen and high carbon dioxide levels.

risks.name: Reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness
risks.summary: All astronauts exercise during their mission to counteract losses in bone density, muscle strength, and heart and blood-vessel performance; researchers study which exercise protects health best.

risks.name: Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS)
risks.summary: The structure of the eyes and brain can change with spaceflight; research targets the long-term consequences and preventing the changes.

risks.name: Spaceflight-induced bone changes
risks.summary: Without gravity, bones break down and become more brittle, raising the chance of painful breaks; research aims to quantify losses and preserve bone strength through diet, exercise and medication.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page: attributes the change to absence of gravity

risks.name: Behavioral changes and psychiatric disorders
risks.summary: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth and other intense stressors may all take a toll on crew mental health; research aims to understand and quantify these risks.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page names distance from Earth

risks.name: Inadequate teamwork
risks.summary: Selecting crews that work well together is essential; researchers study how teams in prolonged isolation and confinement function efficiently, recover after setbacks, and avoid miscommunication and tension.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page names prolonged isolation and confinement

risks.name: Inadequate sleep and irregular schedules
risks.summary: Crews face several hazards at once; stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands and irregular internal body clocks, and reducing their effects is ongoing research.

risks.name: Inadequate systems operations support
risks.summary: Future deep-space crews may face unexpected software, vehicle or other system problems; research targets when crews need information, what training they need and other support options.

risks.name: Injury from dynamic loads
risks.summary: Crews risk injury during landing; understanding how likely it is and how to prevent it is ongoing research.

risks.name: Radiation-induced cancers
risks.summary: Crews exposed to space radiation may be more likely to develop cancer; finding the best mitigation and helpful interventions are ongoing research priorities.

hazardLinks.basis: risks page: risk comes from radiation from space

operationalFacts.fact: JAXA says in-flight health management for astronauts is done remotely, mainly by its designated flight surgeon at NASA Mission Control Houston and by the medical management team at Tsukuba Space Center.
That team manages ISS astronauts' health using medical data that includes interviews, examinations and tests, along with physical performance, nutrition and mental health.
During spacewalks, astronauts' ECG recordings and other measurements are monitored in real time from mission control centers on Earth.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: ARCHeR
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Monitored astronaut well-being, activity, and sleep patterns to learn about human health and performance in deep space.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports tracking the distinction between self-reported well-being, activity, and sleep as separate longitudinal observations.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Immune Biomarkers
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Analyzed blood and saliva samples to investigate how deep space changes the immune system.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Shows that immune monitoring may include laboratory samples; do not represent temperature alone as an immune test.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Artemis II Standard Measures
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Collected a consistent set of crew health information for a research data bank.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports standardized, documented, repeated observations; the page does not publish a full schema or values.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Standard Measures
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Collects a consistent set of physiological and psychological measurements to study how spaceflight affects crew.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports a versioned measurement catalog and repeatable collection protocol.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: CIPHER
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: A suite of studies examining multiple body systems to better understand human-body changes while orbiting Earth.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports a multi-system view while cautioning against claiming the app itself reproduces the research.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Brain Fluid Pressure
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Examines relationships between pressure inside the skull and changes to astronauts’ eyes and brain.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports educational links between brain/eye health and research; no simple consumer measurement or threshold is specified.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Venous Haemostasis
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Examines physical differences that may contribute to blood-flow and blood-coagulation changes.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Reference context only; do not derive a blood-clot assessment from routine vitals.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Zero T2
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Studies exercise in space without a treadmill and its relationship to human health and performance for deep-space missions.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports recording assigned exercise sessions as activity context, not an invented pass/fail target.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Altered Immunity
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Analyzed blood, saliva, and urine samples to investigate how spaceflight alters the immune system.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Shows that immune research can rely on samples and laboratory analysis, not a single proxy metric.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Food Physiology
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Investigated whether an enhanced spaceflight diet could help astronauts adapt to space.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Supports nutrition context as a topic; the page does not provide dietary prescriptions.

hrpResearchHighlights.name: Tempus Pro
hrpResearchHighlights.focus: Tested a commercial telemedicine device used to collect and integrate health data, potentially enabling remote near-real-time diagnoses.
hrpResearchHighlights.possibleAppUse: Relevant precedent for data integration; do not imply Cosmos Health has this device or diagnostic capability.

radiationMonitoring.fact: CSA describes CANS as a compact autonomous instrument under continued development to measure neutron radiation exposure in space.
radiationMonitoring.appImplication: Model radiation observations with sensor identity, measurement time interval, and source; do not claim live CANS integration unless implemented.

radiationMonitoring.fact: CSA says CANS is designed to work continuously and autonomously.
radiationMonitoring.appImplication: A sensor record should distinguish continuous/instrument-collected measurements from manually entered readings.

radiationMonitoring.fact: The CSA article states neutron radiation contributes about 30% of total radiation on the ISS. This is a source-specific contextual figure, not a universal dose conversion or individual health limit.
radiationMonitoring.appImplication: If shown, retain the source and ISS context; do not use as a risk score or individual exposure threshold.

radiationMonitoring.fact: The CSA article notes earlier ISS radiation-detection experiments including MOSFET, EVARM, Radi-N, and Radi-N2.
radiationMonitoring.appImplication: Useful as historical technology context; not evidence that these devices are available to the app.

radiationMonitoring.fact: The CANS article describes potential Earth applications as well as spaceflight applications.

spaceScienceRationale.fact: CSA describes ISS science as helping prepare for deep-space destinations and using knowledge gained to improve quality of life on Earth.

CSA identifies longer missions as involving more time in weightlessness, more radiation exposure, longer isolation, increased communication delays, and less reliance on Earth for food, materials, and emergency medical assistance.
CSA describes research into bones, heart, blood vessels, and brain, and potential relevance to health issues on Earth.
The CSA page says studying the body in space can provide information about reduced physical activity and conditions affecting older adults on Earth.

bodyPanels.fn: Supports thinking, mood, behavior, and sleep timing.
bodyPanels.me: Log sleep and mood consistently; use mission-approved behavioral-health check-ins when assigned.
bodyPanels.why: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth and other intense stressors may all take a toll on crew mental health; research aims to understand and quantify these risks. Crews face several hazards at once; stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands and irregular internal body clocks, and reducing their effects is ongoing research.

bodyPanels.fn: Vision depends on the eye and visual pathways.
bodyPanels.me: Use the mission-provided vision check only if assigned; record blurred vision, visual-field changes, headache, onset, and progression.
bodyPanels.why: The structure of the eyes and brain can change with spaceflight; research targets the long-term consequences and preventing the changes.

bodyPanels.fn: Breathing exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide; cabin systems manage the habitat atmosphere.
bodyPanels.me: Check the designated cabin air sensor and note cough, breathlessness, or headache; sensor checks do not replace medical assessment.
bodyPanels.why: Keeping a spacecraft ecosystem safe means managing temperature, pressure and lighting, reducing noise, monitoring microbial communities and tracking immune responses.
bodyPanels.note: NASA's risks page lists no risk specific to breathing or cabin air; text comes from the hazards page (closed environments).

bodyPanels.fn: The cardiovascular system moves blood and adapts to changes in gravity.
bodyPanels.me: Use approved heart-rate and blood-pressure equipment as trained; record full values, posture, timing, symptoms, and comparison to baseline.
bodyPanels.why: Weightlessness alters blood circulation and heart and blood-vessel function, potentially raising the risk of cardiovascular events.

bodyPanels.fn: Immune responses help the body respond to infection and other threats.
bodyPanels.me: Follow the mission symptom-reporting and temperature-check procedure; record onset and relevant exposure.
bodyPanels.why: Spaceflight stresses can reactivate dormant viruses in astronauts, causing rashes and other symptoms; work continues on understanding immune changes.

bodyPanels.fn: Food and fluid intake support energy, health, and performance.
bodyPanels.me: Use assigned food/fluid logs or glucose testing only when part of the individual medical plan; include meal timing and symptoms.
bodyPanels.why: A healthy, balanced diet is essential to crew health and performance; research targets enjoyable, long-lasting, nutritious meals and the consequences of inadequate nutrition.

All astronauts exercise during their mission to counteract losses in bone density, muscle strength, and heart and blood-vessel performance; researchers study which exercise protects health best.

simulationModel.name: Synthetic hazard-pattern demonstration
simulationModel.label: Simulated association index
simulationModel.method: For each included input, calculate the absolute difference from its project-authored default, divided by its project-authored slider span, then expressed from 0 to 100. For each indicator, gather hazard topics from body panels that list that indicator and from the direct mappings below. A hazard value is the average deviation for distinct included indicators mapped to it whose value differs from its synthetic default; unchanged inputs contribute no deviation. This is a deliberately simplified project-authored simulation rule. It is not calibrated or validated, not a probability, personal risk estimate, cause, health-status label, NASA method, or clinical threshold. Slider bounds are used only to normalize the fictional display.
simulationModel.mappingNote: Body-panel links are contextual associations from the cited risk records. Direct indicator mappings are project-authored educational links; sources describe topics and do not validate this model.
simulationModel.zeroState: All included inputs are at their synthetic defaults, so this simulation has no non-zero pattern match. Change a synthetic input to explore contextual links.
simulationModel.noLinksState: No source-linked hazard topic is connected to the changed inputs in the current data. The interface will not guess a hazard.
simulationModel.uncertainty: A highlighted hazard is only the top match in this fictional rule demonstration. It is not evidence that the hazard caused a reading, and the index is not a likelihood or risk estimate.

items.name: Space Station
items.description: A permanently crewed orbital habitat with regular resupply, real-time ground support, and established medical protocols.

environmentNotes.ex: Daily exercise is critical to combat bone and muscle loss in microgravity.
environmentNotes.sleep: 16 sunrises per day disrupt circadian rhythm; consistent sleep schedule is essential.
environmentNotes.mood: Long-duration confinement with the same crew requires proactive mental health management.
environmentNotes.co2: Cabin CO2 tends to accumulate near sleeping quarters due to limited air circulation.
environmentNotes.call: Regular contact with family and ground teams is readily available — use it.

hazardContext.grav: Primary hazard — continuous microgravity affects all body systems.
hazardContext.iso: Moderate — crew size and Earth views help, but confinement duration matters.
hazardContext.rad: Lower than deep space but still elevated vs Earth; ISS shielding provides protection.
hazardContext.dist: Minimal — Earth is visible and communication is near real-time.
hazardContext.env: Managed life support with regular maintenance; CO2 and microbial monitoring ongoing.

items.name: Deep Space Craft
items.description: A crewed vehicle in transit between Earth and deep-space destinations. Limited volume, no resupply, and communication delays increase self-reliance requirements.
keyFeatures: Communication delay up to 20 minutes each way

environmentNotes.rad: Outside Earth's magnetosphere, radiation exposure increases significantly. Monitor dosimeter readings closely.
environmentNotes.call: Communication delay means real-time conversations aren't possible. Record messages and schedule async contact.
environmentNotes.sleep: No natural light cycle; strict artificial lighting protocol needed for circadian entrainment.
environmentNotes.mood: Extreme isolation from Earth; crew cohesion and mental resilience are critical.
environmentNotes.ex: Exercise equipment is limited; adapt routines to available resistance devices.

hazardContext.rad: Primary hazard — no magnetosphere protection; solar particle events are a serious risk.
hazardContext.dist: Major factor — communication delays up to 20+ minutes; autonomous decision-making required.
hazardContext.iso: High — small crew, no external views of Earth for much of transit, no resupply.
hazardContext.grav: Microgravity throughout transit; exercise countermeasures are essential but equipment-limited.
hazardContext.env: Closed loop life support; any failure is critical with no external support.

items.name: Surface Rover
items.description: A pressurized rover for surface exploration on the Moon or Mars. Short-duration missions from a base, with partial gravity and EVA exposure.
keyFeatures: Dust and radiation exposure during EVAs

environmentNotes.ex: Partial gravity provides some loading but not enough; continue resistance exercise.
environmentNotes.temp: Thermal regulation is challenging in a small pressurized volume; monitor closely.
environmentNotes.rad: Surface radiation is higher than Earth; EVA duration tracking is important.
environmentNotes.sleep: Surface operations may disrupt sleep with mission schedules; protect rest periods.
environmentNotes.hr: Cardiovascular adaptation to partial gravity; monitor for orthostatic intolerance.

hazardContext.grav: Partial gravity (1/6 Moon, 3/8 Mars) — different challenges than microgravity.
hazardContext.rad: No atmosphere on Moon, thin on Mars; surface radiation is a significant concern.
hazardContext.env: Dust infiltration is a persistent problem; life support works harder in a small volume.
hazardContext.iso: Small crew in confined rover for days; psychological factors matter.
hazardContext.dist: Depends on location — Mars has significant delay, Moon has minimal delay.

items.name: Surface Base
items.description: A permanent or semi-permanent surface habitat on the Moon or Mars. Longest-duration stays with the most self-sufficient operations.

environmentNotes.sleep: Extended stay means circadian rhythm must be maintained without natural light cues.
environmentNotes.mood: Most isolated environment; Earth is just a point of light. Proactive mental health care is essential.
environmentNotes.call: Communication delay varies by location; async messaging becomes the norm.
environmentNotes.ex: Long-term partial gravity effects are unknown; aggressive exercise countermeasures needed.
environmentNotes.rad: Cumulative radiation exposure over months/years is a major health concern.

hazardContext.iso: Primary hazard — most isolated human environment ever inhabited.
hazardContext.dist: Mars: up to 22-minute one-way delay; Moon: near real-time but no rescue possible.
hazardContext.rad: Cumulative exposure over long stays; shielding and storm shelters essential.
hazardContext.grav: Partial gravity long-term effects on bone, muscle, cardiovascular system are unknown.
hazardContext.env: Dust, limited repair capability, closed life support over extended periods.
